legs.result: Disposable-clone fixture patch (control-drain.patch in evidence): the fixture's counting wrapper drains the request body via Request.asInputStream(request).readAllBytes() before delegating to the graceful handler, so the fixture never closes a connection with an unconsumed body in flight. Prediction: 8 of 8 loaded full-class runs pass; any no-bytes failure refutes the attribution. Outcome: 8 of 8 passed under the identical 3-burner load. The patch touches only test fixture code in a disposable clone; no assertion, hit count, marker behavior or client materialization proof changes.

summary: Diagnosis supported by a captured failing exchange and a discriminating control. WHICH SIDE CLOSES: the fixture (server) side closes first, deliberately, milliseconds after answering the POST, because the graceful-rejection path writes the 503 response after reading only the request headers and never consumes the chunked request body; Jetty then shuts down (SHUT_WR) and closes the connection. WHY THE TEST FAILS INTERMITTENTLY: the JDK client's request-body publisher streams the materialized update body on its own schedule. When the body finishes before the close lands, the exchange completes and the marked-503 retry logic runs (passing case, fully traced). When CPU load delays the body by tens of milliseconds, the server's close lands first: the client's remaining body writes hit the closed connection (first chunk write succeeds into the closing socket, terminal chunk write returns EPIPE), and the request dies in the transport with 'HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes' instead of surfacing the marked 503, which the trace shows the client had in fact fully received (739 bytes) on that same connection before the EPIPE. Classification: a fixture-transport race between a reject-and-close server and a streaming client body under load. The production graceful-rejection and retry logic is not implicated: in the failing trace the server wrote the complete marked 503 and the client read it; the failure is entirely on the request-body streaming side. A residual client-robustness question is recorded under unresolved alternatives and is not needed to explain the failures. CONTROL: a predeclared fixture patch that drains the request body in the fixture's counting wrapper before the graceful handler can reject (assertions, hit counting, marker behavior and client materialization proofs unchanged) passed 8 of 8 loaded full-class runs, against 2 failures in 7 loaded unmodified runs the same evening and the roughly 1-in-3 loaded rate of the earlier campaigns. The proposed correction is that fixture patch, delivered as evidence and exercised in a disposable clone; nothing was pushed.
unresolved_alternatives: Client robustness: in the failing trace the JDK client had fully received the marked 503 before the EPIPE, yet the request surfaced a transport IOException. Whether HttpJdkSolrClient or the JDK exchange should let a completed response win over a late request-publisher failure is a genuine design question for the branch owner; it is not needed to explain the test failures and no production change is proposed or exercised by this job.

The drain control changes the fixture to consume bodies a real graceful-shutdown server would not consume. It is proposed as a test-determinism fix, not as a claim about how production servers behave; the alternative of asserting through a non-streaming body where materialization is not the point was not exercised.
